claim: IDE plays key roles in degrading peptides vital in type two diabetes, Alzheimer's, inflammation, and other human diseases.
source: Insulin degrading enzyme (IDE) plays key roles in degrading peptides vital in type two diabetes, Alzheimer's, inflammation, and other human diseases.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract summarizing IDE's biological importance, supported by the broader literature context provided in the introduction.

claim: IDE displays a large opening between the homologous ~55 kDa N- and C-terminal halves to allow selective substrate capture based on size and charge complementarity.
source: revealing that IDE displays a large opening between the homologous ~55 kDa N- and C-terminal halves to allow selective substrate capture based on size and charge complementarity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryoEM structures of open-state IDE presented in the manuscript, particularly Figure 3D showing the electrostatic surface and structural analysis.

claim: Amyloidogenic peptides stabilize the disordered IDE catalytic cleft, thereby inducing selective degradation by substrate-assisted catalysis.
source: We also used cryoEM, X-ray crystallography, SAXS, and HDX-MS to elucidate the molecular basis of how amyloidogenic peptides stabilize the disordered IDE catalytic cleft, thereby inducing selective degradation by substrate-assisted catalysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple structural techniques (cryoEM, crystallography, HDX-MS) showing substrate-induced stabilization of the IDE door subdomain, as shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: IDE processively degrades insulin by stochastically cutting either chain without breaking disulfide bonds.
source: Furthermore, our insulin-bound IDE structures explain how IDE processively degrades insulin by stochastically cutting either chain without breaking disulfide bonds.
evidence: This is supported by the cryoEM and crystal structures of insulin-bound IDE showing unfolded insulin in the catalytic chamber, as presented in Figure 7.

claim: IDE is an evolutionarily conserved, M16 family metalloprotease.
source: Insulin degrading enzyme (IDE) is an evolutionarily conserved, M16 family metalloprotease that controls diverse biological functions in model organisms such as mating and cell division in budding yeast and growth in fruit flies (Adames et al., 1995; Fujita et al., 1994; Galagovsky et al., 2014; Tang, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature establishing IDE's classification and evolutionary conservation.

claim: IDE can effectively degrade insulin, amylin, and glucagon, pancreatic hormones that control blood glucose levels, as well as amyloid β (Aβ).
source: IDE can effectively degrade insulin, amylin, and glucagon, pancreatic hormones that control blood glucose levels, as well as amyloid β (Aβ), a peptide implicated in Alzheimer's disease (Duckworth et al., 1998; Kurochkin et al., 2018; Pivovarova et al., 2016; Tang, 2016; Tundo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature documenting IDE's substrate specificity.

claim: Defects in IDE alter the progression of type two diabetes mellitus and Alzheimer's disease in rodents and are linked to these diseases in humans.
source: Defects in IDE alter the progression of type two diabetes mellitus and Alzheimer's disease in rodents and are linked to these diseases in humans (Farris et al., 2003; Farris et al., 2004; Fuchsberger et al., 2016; Pivovarova et al., 2016; Tang, 2016; Tundo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies linking IDE defects to disease progression.

claim: Two IDE-specific inhibitors improve glucose tolerance.
source: Two IDE-specific inhibitors improve glucose tolerance (Durham et al., 2015; Maianti et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating the effect of IDE inhibitors on glucose tolerance.

claim: IDE overexpression reduces Aβ load in mice.
source: IDE overexpression reduces Aβ load in mice (Leissring et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study showing the effect of IDE overexpression on Aβ levels.

claim: IDE is a 110 kDa zinc metalloprotease that readily dimerizes in solution (Kd =~ 10 nM).
source: IDE is a 110 kDa zinc metalloprotease that readily dimerizes in solution (Kd =~ 10 nM) (Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study characterizing IDE's molecular properties.

claim: IDE has at least two major conformational states in its catalytic cycle; open-state IDE captures substrates and releases products while closed-state IDE performs catalysis.
source: IDE has at least two major conformational states in its catalytic cycle; open-state IDE captures substrates and releases products while closed-state IDE performs catalysis (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a model based on previous structural and biochemical studies, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: All crystal structures of dimeric IDE are in the closed state.
source: Thus far, all crystal structures of dimeric IDE are in the closed state.
evidence: This is supported by the literature review of previous crystallographic studies of IDE.

claim: Each IDE subunit consists of ~55 kDa N- and C-terminal domains, IDE-N and IDE-C.
source: Within the IDE dimer, each IDE subunit consists of ~55 kDa N- and C-terminal domains, IDE-N and IDE-C (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by previous structural studies and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: IDE prefers to degrade peptides that are less than 80 amino acid long.
source: Together, these domains form an enclosed, sizable catalytic chamber, the size of which explains why IDE prefers to degrade peptides that are less than 80 amino acid long (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by previous structural and biochemical studies showing the size constraint of the IDE catalytic chamber.

claim: The high selectivity of IDE is partly achieved by the specific interactions between the IDE catalytic chamber and substrate via size and charge complementarity.
source: Various substrate-bound IDE structures reveal that the high selectivity of IDE is partly achieved by the specific interactions between the IDE catalytic chamber and substrate via size and charge complementarity (Guo et al., 2010; Malito et al., 2008b2008; Manolopoulou et al., 2009; Ralat et al., 2011; Ren et al., 2010; Shen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies of substrate-bound IDE.

claim: The formation of cross-β-sheet between an exposed β-strand in the unfolded substrate and the catalytic cleft in conjunction with the anchoring of the substrate's N-terminus to a site that is ~30 Å away from the catalytic zinc ion explains how IDE selectively cleaves the exposed β-strand distal to the N-terminus of the targeted peptides in a stochastic manner.
source: The formation of cross-β-sheet between an exposed β-strand in the unfolded substrate and the catalytic cleft in conjunction with the anchoring of the substrate's N-terminus of substrate to a site that is ~30 Å away from the catalytic zinc ion explains how IDE selectively cleaves the exposed β-strand distal to the N-terminus of the targeted peptides in a stochastic manner (Shen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous structural study explaining IDE's cleavage mechanism.

claim: The structure of open-state IDE has not been determined until now.
source: Until now, the structure of open-state IDE has not been determined.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study, based on literature review.

claim: IDE processively degrades insulin into two pieces without breaking disulfide bonds.
source: IDE processively degrades insulin into two pieces without breaking these disulfide bonds (Figure 1A) (Manolopoulou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The previously reported crystal structure of insulin-bound IDE reveals how insulin is partially unfolded inside the catalytic chamber of IDE.
source: The previously reported crystal structure of insulin-bound IDE reveals how insulin is partially unfolded inside the catalytic chamber of IDE, the first step in the unfolding and degradation of insulin by IDE (Manolopoulou et al., 2009) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous structural study and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The structure of IDE in complex with the fully unfolded insulin prior to the processive cleavage of insulin has remained unsolved.
source: However, the structure of IDE in complex with the fully unfolded insulin prior to the processive cleavage of insulin has remained unsolved.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Amyloidogenic peptides can form highly toxic oligomers/fibrils, leading to many human disorders.
source: Amyloidogenic peptides such as Aβ can form highly toxic oligomers/fibrils, leading to many human disorders (Chiti and Dobson, 2006; Eisenberg and Jucker, 2012; Merlini and Bellotti, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on amyloid diseases.

claim: A salient feature of many amyloidogenic peptides is their high propensity to unfold, resulting in exposed β-strands that together form cross-β-sheets and then amyloid fibrils.
source: A salient feature of many amyloidogenic peptides is their high propensity to unfold, resulting in exposed β-strands that together form cross-β-sheets and then amyloid fibrils (Eisenberg and Jucker, 2012; Fitzpatrick et al., 2017; Lu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on amyloid structure.

claim: Nucleation to form low-molecular-weight oligomers is a key rate limiting step in the formation of amyloid fibrils.
source: Nucleation to form low-molecular-weight oligomers is a key rate limiting step in the formation of amyloid fibrils (Merlini and Bellotti, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature on amyloid formation kinetics.

claim: IDE selectively degrades certain amyloidogenic peptides, preventing amyloid fibril formation.
source: IDE selectively degrades certain amyloidogenic peptides, preventing amyloid fibril formation (Kurochkin, 2001; Malito et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating IDE's effect on amyloid formation.

claim: IDE achieves selective degradation of amyloidogenic peptides by cutting only the monomeric form of these peptides and cleaving at sites located at the β-strand vital for cross-β-sheet formation.
source: IDE achieves this by cutting only the monomeric form of these peptides and cleaving at sites located at the β-strand vital for cross-β-sheet formation (Malito et al., 2008a; Tang, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on IDE's cleavage specificity.

claim: Based on the absence of electron density for the catalytic zinc ion-containing IDE door subdomain in a previously reported Fab1-bound IDE crystal structure, a hypothesis was put forth that IDE uses substrate-assisted catalysis to recognize amyloidogenic peptides.
source: Based on the absence of electron density for the catalytic zinc ion-containing IDE door subdomain in a previously reported Fab1-bound IDE crystal structure, we have put forth a hypothesis that IDE uses substrate-assisted catalysis to recognize amyloidogenic peptides (McCord et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on a previous structural observation, supported by a citation.

claim: The molecular basis for the recognition of amyloidogenic peptides by IDE remains unsolved.
source: Thus, the molecular basis for the recognition of amyloidogenic peptides by IDE remains unsolved.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Recent advances in cryogenic electron microscopy (cryoEM) have profoundly transformed structural biology, making it possible to obtain near atomic resolution 3D structures that are otherwise difficult to achieve by crystallography.
source: Recent advances in cryogenic electron microscopy (cryoEM) have profoundly transformed structural biology, making it possible to obtain near atomic resolution 3D structures that are otherwise difficult to achieve by crystallography (Henderson, 2015; Merk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on cryoEM advances.

claim: Hydrogen-deuterium exchange coupled with mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) and small angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) have recently become widely used techniques to characterize the high-order structure of proteins and protein complexes under physiological conditions in solution.
source: Hydrogen-deuterium exchange coupled with mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) and small angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) have recently become widely used techniques to characterize the high-order structure of proteins and protein complexes under physiological conditions in solution, nicely complement high-resolution techniques such as crystallography and cryoEM (Blanchet and Svergun, 2013; Marciano et al., 2014; Putnam et al., 2007; Ward et al., 2013; Wei et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on HDX-MS and SAXS methods.

claim: FabH11 bound IDE tightly (~1 nM).
source: FabH11 was chosen because it bound IDE tightly (~1 nM) and only slightly increased IDE activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, including SPR measurements.

claim: FabH11 only slightly increased IDE activity.
source: FabH11 was chosen because it bound IDE tightly (~1 nM) and only slightly increased IDE activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C showing enzymatic activity assays.

claim: The X-ray structure of FabH11-E-bound IDE was determined at 3.8 Å resolution.
source: The resulting molecule, FabH11-E, was then used to determine an X-ray structure of FabH11-E-bound IDE at 3.8 Å resolution (R/Rfree = 22/27%, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The crystal structure of FabH11-E-bound IDE revealed a closed-state IDE dimer that is nearly identical to those reported previously.
source: The crystal structure revealed a closed-state IDE dimer that is nearly identical to those reported previously (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D)(Guo et al., 2010; Malito et al., 2008b2008; Manolopoulou et al., 2009; Ren et al., 2010; Shen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and comparison with previous structures, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: All crystal structures of IDE dimer solved so far are in the closed state, likely due to the constraints imposed by the crystal lattice.
source: All crystal structures of IDE dimer solved so far are in the closed state, likely due to the constraints imposed by the crystal lattice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that only closed-state structures have been obtained by crystallography.

claim: HDX-MS data suggest that FabH11-E binding has a minimal effect on the conformation dynamics or regional stability of IDE in solution.
source: As there is no major change in HDX between IDE alone and FabH11-E-bound IDE that is distal to FabH11-E binding site, our HDX-MS data also suggest that FabH11-E binding has a minimal effect on the conformation dynamics or regional stability of IDE in solution.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplements 2–4.

claim: FabH11-E binding causes a 50% enhancement of IDE catalytic activity.
source: This could explain a 50% enhancement of IDE catalytic activity upon FabH11-E binding (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The cryoEM structures of FabH11-E-bound IDE are likely to represent the conformations of IDE dimer in solution.
source: Thus, the cryoEM structures of FabH11-E-bound IDE is likely to represent the conformations of IDE dimer in solution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the HDX-MS data showing minimal perturbation by Fab binding.

claim: A cryoEM map of the insulin-bound IDE-FabH11-E was constructed using 218,162 particles initially, refined, and solved at 4.1 Å resolution.
source: A cryoEM map of the insulin-bound IDE-FabH11-E was constructed using 218,162 particles initially, refined, and solved at 4.1 Å resolution, which confirms how FabH11-E binds IDE (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 8B, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by cryoEM data and processing statistics presented in the manuscript.

claim: The resolution of the insulin-bound IDE dimer was improved to 3.7 Å using IDE dimer-focused classification with signal subtraction and refinement.
source: We further improved the resolution of the IDE dimer using IDE dimer-focused classification with signal subtraction and refinement, resulting in a map and structural model with an overall resolution of 3.7 Å (Figure 2—figure supplements 8B, 9 and 10, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by cryoEM data processing and refinement statistics.

claim: Apo FabH11-E-bound IDE showed a highly preferred orientation in vitreous ice.
source: Apo FabH11-E-bound IDE showed a highly preferred orientation in vitreous ice.
evidence: This is an observation from cryoEM data collection.

claim: Images were acquired with the grid tilted at an angle to the electron beam to allow better sampling of other orientations.
source: Thus, images were acquired with the grid tilted at an angle to the electron beam, which allowed better sampling of other orientations (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 9B) (Tan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a methodological approach used to address preferred orientation, supported by a citation.

claim: The initial 3D refinement of apo IDE-FabH11-E of 151,868 particles had a resolution of 4.4 Å.
source: The initial 3D refinement of apo IDE-FabH11-E of 151,868 particles had a resolution of 4.4 Å.
evidence: This is supported by cryoEM data processing statistics.

claim: Further 3D classification revealed three major conformations of apo-IDE.
source: Further 3D classification revealed three major conformations and structural models were built (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by cryoEM data processing and classification results.

claim: The three apo-IDE structures derive from combinations of the IDE partial open (pO) and open (O) states.
source: The three apo-IDE structures derive from combinations of the IDE partial open (pO) and open (O) states (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by cryoEM structural analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The dimer with one open and one partially open conformational subunit (open/partial open, 110,499 particles) reached an overall resolution of 4.2 Å.
source: The dimer with one open and one partially open conformational subunit (open/partial open, 110,499 particles) reached an overall resolution of 4.2 Å (Figure 3A, Figure 2—figure supplements 5–9, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by cryoEM data processing and refinement statistics.

claim: The dimer with two open conformational subunits (open/open, 24,425 particles) resulted in an overall resolution of 6.5 Å.
source: The dimer with two open conformational subunits (open/open, 24,425 particles) resulted in an overall resolution of 6.5 Å (Figure 3A, Figure 2—figure supplements 5–9, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by cryoEM data processing and refinement statistics.

claim: The dimer with two partially open conformational subunits (partial open/partial open, 16,944 particles) reached 6.9 Å resolution.
source: The dimer with two partially open conformational subunits (partial open/partial open, 16,944 particles) reached 6.9 Å resolution (Figure 3A, Figure 2—figure supplements 5–9, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by cryoEM data processing and refinement statistics.

claim: The conformation of pO and O states in the pO/O IDE dimer differ significantly from those in pO/pO or O/O IDE dimer.
source: Interestingly, the conformation of pO and O states in the pO/O IDE dimer differ significantly from those in pO/pO or O/O IDE dimer.
evidence: This is an observation from structural analysis of the cryoEM structures.

claim: Two subunits within O/O or pO/pO states have noticeable differences in the distance and buried surface between IDE-N and IDE-C and the dihedral angle.
source: Furthermore, two subunits within O/O or pO/pO states have noticeable differences in the distance and buried surface between IDE-N and IDE-C and the dihedral angle (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis data presented in Supplementary file 4.

claim: Open-state IDE has an opening just wide enough to capture its substrates, allowing the IDE catalytic chamber to attract these substrates with high dipole moment via charge complementarity.
source: Open-state IDE has an opening just wide enough to capture its substrates, for example, insulin, TGF-α, and MIP-1α/β, allowing the IDE catalytic chamber to attract these substrates with high dipole moment via charge complementarity (Figure 3D) (Guo et al., 2010; Manolopoulou et al., 2009; Ren et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3D and citations to previous studies.

claim: SAXS data showed that IDE in solution exist in equilibrium between open and partially open states and that insulin constrained the IDE dimer into mostly partially closed or closed states.
source: Our SAXS data showed that IDE in solution exist in equilibrium between open and partially open states and that insulin constrained the IDE dimer into mostly partially closed or closed states.
evidence: This is supported by SAXS data presented in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The change in Rg value caused by the rapid mixing of IDE with insulin fit well with a single exponential decay with τ = 0.1 s.
source: We found that the change in Rg value caused by the rapid mixing of IDE with insulin fit well with a single exponential decay with τ = 0.1 s (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by time-resolved SAXS data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The timeframe required for insulin to induce conformational switching from a high Rg state to a low Rg state is close to the rate of degradation of insulin by IDE (~2 s−1).
source: Thus, the timeframe required for insulin to induce conformational switching from a high Rg state to a low Rg state is close to the rate of degradation of insulin by IDE (~2 s−1).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the SAXS-derived rate constant with the known enzymatic rate.

claim: Insulin-induced IDE open-closed transition is likely a key rate-limiting step for insulin clearance by IDE.
source: This suggests that insulin-induced IDE open-closed transition is likely a key rate-limiting step for insulin clearance by IDE.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of conformational change rate with enzymatic rate.

claim: Crystal structures for Fab1-bound IDE structures in the presence of Aβ and insulin were solved at 3.5 Å and 3.9 Å resolution, respectively.
source: We thus solved crystal structures for Fab1-bound IDE structures in the presence of Aβ and insulin at 3.5 Å and 3.9 Å resolution, respectively (R/Rfree = 23/27%, R/free = 24/29%) and Fab1E- and insulin-bound IDE at 3.3 Å resolution (R/Rfree = 20/25%) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and refinement statistics.

claim: The door subdomain of IDE is clearly visible in substrate-bound IDE crystal structures.
source: Instead of being absent, as in the apo-IDE crystal structure (McCord et al., 2013), we found that the door subdomain of IDE is clearly visible in these structures (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: These IDE structures are nearly identical to closed-state IDE determined in the previously reported insulin- or Aβ-bound IDE (RMSD = 0.46 and 0.56 Å, respectively).
source: In fact, these IDE structures are nearly identical to closed-state IDE determined in the previously reported insulin- or Aβ-bound IDE (RMSD = 0.46 and 0.56 Å, respectively, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The IDE door subdomain, particularly the catalytic zinc-coordinating α4 helix, has significantly higher thermal B factors in apo-IDE than in insulin-bound IDE.
source: Indeed, while clearly visible, the IDE door subdomain, particularly the catalytic zinc-coordinating α4 helix, has significantly higher thermal B factors than in the insulin-bound structure (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by B-factor analysis of cryoEM structures shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The presence of insulin profoundly reduces the thermal B factors of IDE door subdomain.
source: The presence of insulin thus profoundly reduces the thermal B factors of IDE door subdomain (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by B-factor analysis comparing apo and insulin-bound IDE structures.

claim: Both BDM44768 and 6bK inhibitors decreased HDX in the IDE door subdomain.
source: In addition to the expected HDX reduction where BDM44768 and 6bK directly bind, both inhibitors also decreased HDX in the IDE door subdomain (Figure 5C and D, Figure 5—figure supplements 3–6).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Multiple regions in IDE exhibited a significant reduction in HDX upon insulin binding.
source: Multiple regions in IDE exhibited a significant reduction in HDX upon insulin binding (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 6A and supplementary figures.

claim: Insulin binding reduced HDX in known substrate-binding sites of IDE: the door subdomain, exosite in domain D2, and residues 821–830 in domain D4.
source: These include known substrate-binding sites of IDE: the door subdomain that contains the zinc catalytic site in domain D1, exosite in domain D2 that anchors the N-terminal region of IDE substrates, and residues 821–830 in domain D4 that binds the P1' and P2' residues of IDE substrates after the scissile bond (McCord et al., 2013; Shen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data and citations to previous structural studies identifying these binding sites.

claim: Insulin also reduced HDX in regions that directly bind IDE door subdomain including the hydrophobic rich H loop, residues 668–673 and residues 821–830.
source: Insulin also reduced HDX in regions that directly bind IDE door subdomain including the hydrophobic rich H loop, residues 668–673 and residues 821–830 (McCord et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Insulin binding reduced the HDX at the IDE-N and IDE-C joining loop and its underlying α-helices, α11 and α20.
source: Furthermore, insulin binding also reduced the HDX at the IDE-N and IDE-C joining loop and its underlying α-helices, α11 and α20, which is consistent with our SAXS data showing that insulin facilitates the open-closed transition of IDE.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data and is consistent with SAXS data.

claim: A similar pattern of HDX reduction in IDE was also observed when IDE was mixed with Aβ1-40.
source: A similar pattern of HDX reduction in IDE was also observed when IDE was mixed with Aβ1-40 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Insulin stabilizes the entire IDE door subdomain (residues 170–237) while Aβ only stabilizes the zinc-binding portion of IDE door subdomain (residues 170–203).
source: For example, insulin stabilizes the entire IDE door subdomain (residues 170–237) while Aβ only stabilizes the zinc-binding portion of IDE door subdomain (residues 170–203) (Figure 6—figure supplements 3–4).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data comparing insulin and Aβ binding effects.

claim: The binding of substrates promotes the open to closed transition of IDE and stabilizes the IDE catalytic site for substrate-assisted catalysis.
source: Together, our data indicate that the binding of substrates promotes the open to closed transition of IDE and stabilizes the IDE catalytic site for substrate-assisted catalysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the integration of HDX-MS, SAXS, and structural data.

claim: Extra electron density was clearly visible inside the IDE catalytic chamber in cryoEM and crystal structures of insulin-bound IDE.
source: In our cryoEM and crystal structures of insulin-bound IDE, extra electron density was clearly visible inside the IDE catalytic chamber (Figure 7B and C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 7B, C and supplementary figures.

claim: The insulin structure in the new structures is quite different to that reported previously.
source: and the insulin structure is quite different to that reported previously (Manolopoulou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with a previous structure, cited.

claim: The extra density fit well with regions of an unfolded insulin A or B chain with a known scissile bond properly residing at the IDE catalytic site.
source: The extra density fit well with regions of an unfolded insulin A or B chain with a known scissile bond properly residing at the IDE catalytic site (Figure 7A and B, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling and fitting shown in Figure 7 and supplementary figures.

claim: The density has key features that can be contributed by either insulin chain and can be best interpreted as an ensemble of unfolded insulin A and B chains.
source: Thus, this density has key features that can be contributed by either chain and can be best interpreted as an ensemble of unfolded insulin A and B chains, not belonging solely to either chain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data based on the observed electron density features.

claim: Upon insulin capture by IDE catalytic chamber, IDE stochastically cuts whichever of either insulin A or B chain binds the IDE catalytic cleft first after insulin unfolding inside the catalytic chamber.
source: Upon insulin capture by IDE catalytic chamber, IDE stochastically cuts whichever of either insulin A or B chain binds the IDE catalytic cleft first after insulin unfolding inside the catalytic chamber (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on the structural data showing both chains can fit in the catalytic site.

claim: The N-terminus of insulin interacts extensively with the IDE-N exosite while IDE-C makes substantial contacts with the C-terminal part of insulin.
source: Our structures also reveal that the N-terminus of insulin interacts extensively with the IDE-N exosite while IDE-C makes substantial contacts with the C-terminal part of insulin.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of insulin-bound IDE structures.

claim: The N- and C-terminal parts of the singly-cut insulin are still joined by the inter-molecular disulfide bond, allowing insulin to still effectively keep IDE in the closed conformation.
source: As the N- and C-terminal parts of insulin of the singly-cut insulin are still joined by the inter-molecular disulfide bond, insulin could still effectively keep IDE in the closed conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation of disulfide bond connectivity.

claim: The subsequent unfolding of cleaved insulin leads to processive cleavage of the other insulin chain.
source: The subsequent unfolding of cleaved insulin leads to processive cleavage of the other insulin chain (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on the structural data and known processivity of insulin degradation.

claim: By rigid-body motion between IDE-N and IDE-C, IDE switches between O and pO states.
source: By rigid-body motion between IDE-N and IDE-C, IDE switches between O and pO states.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on structural analysis of different IDE conformational states.

claim: Only open-state IDE captures large peptide substrates (e.g. insulin and Aβ).
source: Only open-state IDE captures large peptide substrates (e.g. insulin and Aβ).
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the structural analysis showing the opening required for substrate entry.

claim: The degree of opening and the charge distribution of the IDE catalytic chamber determine which peptides are captured by IDE depending on their size and high dipole moment.
source: The degree of opening and the charge distribution of the IDE catalytic chamber determine which peptides are captured by IDE depending on their size and high dipole moment (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on structural analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The motions between open- and closed-state IDE, in conjunction with the selective interactions of the IDE catalytic chamber with these peptides, creates a force to selectively unfold amyloidogenic peptides.
source: The motions between open- and closed-state IDE, in conjunction with the selective interactions of the IDE catalytic chamber with these peptides, for example, IDE exosite with peptide's N-terminus, creates a force to selectively unfold amyloidogenic peptides.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on the structural data and HDX-MS data.

claim: The exposed β-strand of amyloidogenic peptides stabilizes the inherently unstable IDE catalytic center, leading to the degradation of amyloidogenic peptides by IDE.
source: The exposed β-strand of these peptides then stabilizes the inherently unstable IDE catalytic center, leading to the degradation of amyloidogenic peptides by IDE.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the substrate-assisted catalysis model supported by structural and HDX-MS data.

claim: The preferred O/pO combination indicates that the motion of IDE-N in one subunit of IDE dimer is not independent from the other.
source: Furthermore, the preferred O/pO combination indicates that the motion of IDE-N in one subunit of IDE dimer is not independent from the other (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed distribution of conformational states in the cryoEM data.

claim: The substrate-induced closure of one subunit can promote the switch of the other subunit to the open state, allowing cleaved products to be released or substrate captured.
source: We thus envision that the preferred combination of the open and 'closed' states within the IDE dimer would allow the substrate-induced closure of one subunit to promote the switch of the other subunit to the open state, allowing cleaved products to be released or substrate captured (Video 3 synchronized motion 1).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on the observed conformational distribution and allostery.

claim: The opening of one subunit from the 'closed'-state will promote the closure of the other for substrate unfolding and catalysis.
source: Conversely, the opening of one subunit from the 'closed'-state will promote the closure of the other for substrate unfolding and catalysis (Video 3 synchronized motion 1).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on the observed conformational distribution and allostery.

claim: Such motions can explain how substrate allosterically regulates IDE activity and how monomerization mutations render IDE less active as well as the lose the ATP- and substrate-mediated regulation.
source: Such motions can explain how substrate allosterically regulates IDE activity and how monomerization mutations render IDE less active as well as the lose the ATP- and substrate-mediated regulation (Ralat et al., 2011; Song et al., 2003; Song et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the structural observations to previous biochemical data, supported by citations.

claim: This model is consistent with kinetic studies which show that phenylalanine 530 mutation to alanine at the linker joining IDE-N and IDE-C makes IDE hyperactive and alters allosteric regulation.
source: This model is also consistent with the kinetic studies which show that phenylalanine 530 mutation to alanine at the linker joining IDE-N and IDE-C makes IDE hyperactive and alters allosteric regulation (McCord et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study showing the effect of this mutation.

claim: HDX-MS data reveal that the binding of IDE substrate or inhibitor only affects the deuterium exchange at the IDE-N and IDE interface and the linker between IDE-N and IDE-C, not between the interface of two IDE subunits.
source: Our HDX-MS data reveal that the binding of IDE substrate or inhibitor only affects the deuterium exchange at the IDE-N and IDE interface and the linker between IDE-N and IDE-C, not between the interface of two IDE subunits (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: IDE allostery is mediated by the collective motions of many atoms in IDE, not by a subset of atoms within a defined path.
source: We speculate that IDE allostery is mediated by the collective motions of many atoms in IDE, not by a subset of atoms within a defined path.
evidence: This is speculation based on the lack of an obvious allosteric pathway in the HDX-MS data.

claim: CryoEM is uniquely capable of solving the structures of large flexible macro-molecules.
source: CryoEM is uniquely capable of solving the structures of these large flexible macro-molecules.
evidence: This is a general statement about cryoEM capabilities, supported by the broader literature.

claim: Improvements in hardware technology over the past 5 years now provide for excellent quality images.
source: Improvements in the hardware technology over the past 5 years (Li et al., 2013) now provide for excellent quality images
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature on cryoEM technology advances.

claim: Improvements in software allow for classification of particles of different conformations from a heterogeneous mixture of structures.
source: and improvements in software allow for classification of particles of different conformations from a heterogeneous mixture of structures (Scheres, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature on cryoEM software development.

claim: Spotiton allows preparation of samples embedded in a very thin and even layer of vitrified ice, which improves data quality.
source: A new vitrification device, Spotiton, allows us to prepare samples embedded in a very thin and even layer of vitrified ice, which improves data quality (Dandey et al., 2018; Razinkov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on Spotiton technology.

claim: Acquiring images from gold-coated grids tilted relative to the electron beam addresses the issues of preferred orientation.
source: We also addressed the issues of preferred orientation, quite common for many samples, by acquiring images from gold-coated grids tilted relative to the electron beam (Russo and Passmore, 2014; Tan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on addressing preferred orientation in cryoEM.

claim: The accumulation of toxic amyloid fibrils is associated with many human diseases.
source: The accumulation of toxic amyloid fibrils is associated with many human diseases and IDE plays a key role in preventing amyloid fibril formation by its proteolytic activities (Jucker and Walker, 2013; Tang, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on amyloid diseases.

claim: IDE plays a key role in preventing amyloid fibril formation by its proteolytic activities.
source: The accumulation of toxic amyloid fibrils is associated with many human diseases and IDE plays a key role in preventing amyloid fibril formation by its proteolytic activities (Jucker and Walker, 2013; Tang, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on IDE's role in amyloid prevention.

claim: Accumulating data suggest that IDE plays non-proteolytic roles to regulate other proteostatic processes, for example, regulating proteasome activity and preventing amyloid fibril formation of α-synuclein.
source: Accumulating data also suggest that IDE plays non-proteolytic roles to regulate other proteostatic processes, for example, regulating proteasome activity and preventing amyloid fibril formation of α-synuclein (Tang, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous review on IDE functions.

claim: Substrate selective modulation of IDE activity is crucial to realize IDE-based therapy.
source: As IDE modulates proteostasis by targeting diverse proteins, substrate selective modulation of IDE activity is crucial to realize IDE-based therapy (Pivovarova et al., 2016; Tang, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on IDE as a therapeutic target.

claim: Noticeable differences in the reduction of HDX between insulin- and Aβ-bound IDE exist.
source: Indeed, noticeable differences in the reduction of HDX between insulin- and Aβ-bound IDE exist (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: The cryoEM structure of the insulin-bound IDE dimer at 3.7 Å resolution shows that both IDE subunits adopt a similar but not identical partially closed (pC) state.
source: The cryoEM structure of the insulin-bound IDE dimer at 3.7 Å resolution (Videos 1–2) shows that both IDE subunits adopt a similar but not identical partially closed (pC) state that differs from the previously reported closed-state IDE (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 4) (Guo et al., 2010; Malito et al., 2008b2008; Manolopoulou et al., 2009; Ren et al., 2010; Shen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by cryoEM structural data shown in Figure 3B and supplementary materials.

claim: The buried surface area between IDE-N and IDE-C and distance between center of mass (COM) of D1 and D4 in the cryoEM pC state is nearly identical to those in the closed-state IDE shown by X-ray crystallographic studies.
source: The buried surface area between IDE-N and IDE-C and distance between center of mass (COM) of D1 and D4 in the cryoEM pC state is nearly identical to those in the closed-state IDE shown by X-ray crystallographic studies (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis data shown in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 4.

claim: The pC state has an approximately 2° decreased dihedral angle between the COM of four homologous domains, D1-D4, compared to those in the closed-state IDE.
source: However, this pC state has an approximately 2° decreased dihedral angle between the COM of four homologous domains, D1-D4, compared to those in the closed-state IDE (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 4), suggesting a potential gliding motion allows IDE to shift between partially closed and closed states.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis data shown in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 4.

claim: Both IDE pC and C states are catalytically competent.
source: Thus, both IDE pC and C states are catalytically competent.
evidence: This is an inference based on the position of insulin in the catalytic cleft in the pC state structure.

claim: The IDE pO and O states differs from the pC and C states by 5 Å to 24 Å increases in the distance between D1 and D4 and 7° to 17° increases in the dihedral angle, respectively.
source: The IDE pO and O states differs from the pC and C states by 5 Å to 24 Å increases in the distance between D1 and D4 and 7° to 17° increases in the dihedral angle, respectively (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 4, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis data shown in Figure 3B and supplementary materials.

claim: These changes result in decreased buried surface between IDE-N and IDE-C in pO and O states.
source: These changes result in decreased buried surface between IDE-N and IDE-C in pO and O states.
evidence: This is a direct consequence of the structural changes observed in the cryoEM structures.

claim: The three conformers have resolution limits which correlated well with their relative populations: O/pO (4.2 Å, 73%), O/O (6.5 Å, 16%), and pO/pO (6.9 Å, 11%).
source: The three conformers have resolution limits which correlated well with their relative populations: O/pO (4.2 Å, 73%), O/O (6.5 Å, 16%), and pO/pO (6.9 Å, 11%).
evidence: This is supported by cryoEM data processing and particle distribution statistics.

claim: Two subunits within O/O or pO/pO states have noticeable differences in the distance and buried surface between IDE-N and IDE-C and the dihedral angle, providing a potential explanation for the mechanism by which dimerization-induced allostery regulates the catalytic activity of IDE.
source: Furthermore, two subunits within O/O or pO/pO states have noticeable differences in the distance and buried surface between IDE-N and IDE-C and the dihedral angle (Supplementary file 4). Such differences provide a potential explanation for the mechanism by which dimerization-induced allostery regulates the catalytic activity of IDE (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (McCord et al., 2013; Ralat et al., 2011; Song et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis and supported by citations to previous studies on IDE allostery.

claim: Enzyme kinetic analysis estimated that insulin degradation by IDE occurs reasonably rapidly, up to ~2 per second.
source: Enzyme kinetic analysis estimated that insulin degradation by IDE occurs reasonably rapidly, up to ~2 per second (Manolopoulou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous kinetic study.

claim: IDE readily dimerizes (Kd = 10 nM).
source: By the extensive contacts between IDE-C domains, IDE readily dimerizes (Kd =~ 10 nM) (Li et al., 2006; Shen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies characterizing IDE dimerization.

claim: CryoEM data reveal that two IDE-N domains within the IDE dimer undergoes rigid body motion, allowing IDE to undergo the transition between the open and 'closed' states without the assistance of substrate.
source: Our cryoEM data reveal that two IDE-N domains within the IDE dimer undergoes rigid body motion, allowing IDE to undergo the transition between the open and 'closed' states without the assistance of substrate (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by cryoEM structural data showing multiple conformational states of apo-IDE.
